## The Coin Problem {.scrollable}
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}

An article in The Guardian stated: _When spun on edge 250 times, a Belgian one-euro coin came up heads 140 times and tails 110._

:::{.center-text}
<img src="images/map/euro-coin.png" width=200/>
:::

__Questions__:

1. Find the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate for the probability of heads.
2. How do different choices for the prior influence the MAP estimate?

:::

## Learning Objectives {.scrollable}
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}

- Likelihood of the entire data set
- Priors
    - Uninformative
    - Informative

:::

## Review: Bayesian Updating {.scrollable}
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}

Last lecture we wrote the Bayesian update in terms of _**distributions**_:

$$
\text{posterior} \propto \text{prior} \times \text{likelihood}
$$

1. Multiply the prior by the likelihood of the data.
2. Divide by the sum so the probabilities add up to 1.

<br>

When we get **more data**, the posterior becomes the new prior and we simply update again.

__Extended cookie problem__: 101 bowls, bowl $i$ is $i\%$ vanilla, uniform prior.

- Draw vanilla &rarr; higher-numbered bowls become more likely; bowl 0 drops to 0.
- Draw vanilla again &rarr; the posterior shifts even further toward high-numbered bowls.
- Draw chocolate &rarr; bowl 100 drops to 0, and the peak moves back toward the middle.

:::

## Review: Maximum A Posteriori Estimator {.scrollable}
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}

```{python}
def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
     <span class="label">Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) Estimate</span>
        <p>
         The maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate is the hypothesis that maximizes the posterior probability.
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```

In Python, we find it with `dist['probs'].idxmax()`.

- __Cookies__: after drawing vanilla, vanilla, chocolate, the MAP is **Bowl 67**, the bowl closest to the observed proportion $2/3$ vanilla. With a uniform prior, the MAP matches the proportion in the data.
- __Monty Hall__: you pick door 1 and Monty opens door 3. The posteriors are $1/3$, $2/3$, and $0$ for doors 1, 2, and 3. The MAP is **door 2**, so you should switch.

<br>

Today we ask: _**what happens to the MAP when we change the prior?**_

:::

## Estimating Proportions {.scrollable}
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
The cookie problem with 101 bowls is equivalent to a more typical question about the proportion of vanilla cookies in one bowl:

<br><br>

_Imagine that you have one bowl of chocolate and vanilla cookies. You don't know what fraction of cookies are vanilla, but you think it is equally likely to be any fraction from 0 to 1. If you draw three cookies and two are vanilla, what proportion of cookies in the bowl do you think are vanilla?_
:::

## The Coin Problem {.scrollable}
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}

We can approach this problem just like the extended cookie problem.

```{python}
# distribution version of update from the previous lecture
def update(distribution, likelihood):
    '''perform a Bayesian update on distribution using likelihood'''
    distribution['probs'] = distribution['probs'] * likelihood
    prob_data = distribution['probs'].sum()
    distribution['probs'] = distribution['probs'] / prob_data
    return distribution
```

```{python}
#| echo: true
p_dist = pd.DataFrame(index = np.arange(101)/100)

# uniform prior distribution
p_dist['probs'] = randint(0, 101).pmf(np.arange(101))
p_dist_batch = p_dist.copy()  # copy of the uniform prior for the single-update approach

# likelihoods
likelihood_heads = np.arange(101) / 100
likelihood_tails = 1 - likelihood_heads
```

:::{.center-text}
```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 2.5))
plt.plot(np.arange(101)/100, likelihood_heads, 'green', label = 'P(Heads | p)', lw = 4)
plt.plot(np.arange(101)/100, likelihood_tails, 'red', label = 'P(Tails | p)', lw = 4)
plt.legend(loc = 'best', fontsize = 14)
plt.xlabel('$p$', size = 16)
plt.ylabel('Probability', size = 16)
plt.title('Likelihoods', size = 20)
plt.show()
```
:::
:::

## The Coin Problem {.scrollable}
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
Let's represent the data from the problem. There are 140 heads and 110 tails. It doesn't matter what order they occur in.

```{python}
#| echo: true
data = 'H' * 140 + 'T' * 110
data
```

```{python}
#| echo: true
for item in data:
    if item == 'H':
        update(p_dist, likelihood_heads)
    elif item == 'T':
        update(p_dist, likelihood_tails)
    else:
        print('Bad data!')
```

## The Coin Problem {.scrollable}

:::{.center-text}
```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3))
p_dist.plot(ax=ax, lw=4, legend=False, title='Posterior Distribution of $p$', fontsize=14)
ax.set_xlabel('$p$', size=14)
ax.set_ylabel('Probability', size=14)
plt.show()
```
:::

This figure shows the posterior distribution of $p$, the probability of heads for the euro coin that was spun.

The posterior reflects updated beliefs about $p$ after observing the data, indicating that values below 0.4 and above 0.7 are unlikely, while values between approximately 0.5 and 0.6 are most probable.
:::

## The Coin Problem {.scrollable}
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
_**What is the MAP estimate in this case?**_

```{python}
#| echo: true
p_dist['probs'].idxmax()
```

The MAP is 0.56, which is also the proportion of heads in the dataset, $140/250$. This gives an answer to our first question about the coin.

<br>

We obtained our answer using the uniform prior, the prior that assigns the same prior probability to each hypothesis. The uniform prior essentially makes no a priori assumption about the values of the parameter being estimated. For that reason, it is often called an __uninformative__ prior.

Will this answer change if we select a different prior?
:::

## Priors {.scrollable}
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}

In the Bayesian view, we are using probability to represent our _**confidence**_ across different hypotheses.

The role of the prior is to represent our level of confidence, or our state of knowledge, _**before seeing any data.**_

Based on what we know about coins, if a coin is lopsided, $p$ might deviate from $\frac{1}{2}$. However, it seems unlikely that the Belgian euro coin is so imbalanced that $p$ might be 0.1 or 0.9.

It might be more reasonable to choose a prior that gives higher probability to values of $p$ near $\frac{1}{2}$ and lower probability to extreme values.

As an example, let's try a _**triangle-shaped**_ prior. Such a prior is considered _**informative**_, because we are using our knowledge about coins to construct it.

:::

## Triangle-Shaped Prior {.scrollable}
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
```{python}
#| echo: true
triangle_prior = np.append(np.arange(50), np.arange(50, -1, -1))
triangle_prior = triangle_prior / np.sum(triangle_prior)

p_dist_tri = pd.DataFrame(index = np.arange(101)/100)
p_dist_tri['probs'] = triangle_prior
```

:::{.center-text}
```{python}
p_dist_tri.plot(lw = 4, legend = False, title = 'Triangle-shaped Prior for $p$', fontsize = 14, figsize=(6,4))
plt.xlabel('$p$', size = 14)
plt.ylabel('Probability', size = 14)
plt.show()
```
:::
:::

## Priors {.scrollable}
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
Let's compute the posterior distribution starting from this prior.

```{python}
#| echo: true
update(p_dist_tri, likelihood);
```

:::{.center-text}
```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8,3))
p_dist_tri.plot(ax = ax, color = 'cornflowerblue', lw = 4, fontsize = 14)
p_dist.plot(ax = ax, color = 'orange', lw = 4, style = '--', fontsize = 14)
ax.legend(['Posterior (triangle prior)', 'Posterior (uniform prior)'], fontsize = 14, loc = 'best')
plt.xlabel('$p$', size = 16)
plt.ylabel('Probability', size = 16)
plt.show()
```
:::

## Swamping The Prior {.scrollable}
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}

- The posterior distributions are nearly identical under the two priors.
- Although different individuals may start with different beliefs about the coin's bias, the data dominate the analysis.
- With a large sample size (250 observations), the influence of the prior becomes negligible.
- As a result, different prior beliefs lead to essentially the same posterior distribution.
- This effect is known as __swamping the prior__: with sufficient data, posteriors converge despite differing priors.

:::

## Group Question 1 {.scrollable}
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}

```{python}
def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="blue-box">
        <p>
        You have a coin with uncertain fairness. You consider the following probabilities of heads, \(p\): 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, and 1. You flip the coin 10 times and observe 7 heads.<br>
        a. Using the uniform prior, compute the posterior probabilities for the five values of \(p\) that are being considered. Provide your final answer using a full Bayes table.
        <br>
        <br>
        <br>
        <br>
        <br>
        <br>
        <br>
        <br>
        <br>
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```

:::

:::{.notes}
**Solution (a)**: Likelihood of 7 heads in 10 flips: $P(D \mid p) = \binom{10}{7} p^7 (1-p)^3 = 120\, p^7 (1-p)^3$.

| $p$ | Prior | Likelihood | Unnorm. post. | Posterior |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0.2 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 0.25 | 0.2 | 0.0031 | 0.0006 | 0.0083 |
| 0.5 | 0.2 | 0.1172 | 0.0234 | 0.3162 |
| 0.75 | 0.2 | 0.2503 | 0.0501 | 0.6754 |
| 1 | 0.2 | 0 | 0 | 0 |

Total probability of the data: 0.0741.

$p = 0$ and $p = 1$ get posterior 0 because we saw both heads and tails. The $\binom{10}{7}$ factor cancels when normalizing, so students who leave it out get the same posteriors.
:::

**Solution (b)**: The MAP estimate is $p = 0.75$, with posterior probability 0.6754. It is the grid value closest to the observed proportion of heads, $7/10 = 0.7$.
:::

## Group Question 2 {.scrollable}
:::{style="font-size: .75em"}

```{python}
def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="blue-box">
        <p>
        A magician has a bag containing 30 coins that all look identical. However, there are actually three types of coins: \(A\), \(B\), and \(C\).
        <ul>
            <li>10 coins of type \(A\) are biased, with \(P(H \mid A) = 3/5\).</li>
            <li>5 coins of type \(B\) are biased, with \(P(H \mid B) = 1/10\).</li>
            <li>15 coins of type \(C\) are fair, with \(P(H \mid C) = 1/2\).</li>
        </ul>
        The magician takes a coin from the bag at random and flips it. The result is heads.<br><br>
        a. Fill out the Bayes table below to find the posterior probability of each coin type. Also give the value of the normalizer (the total probability of the data).
        <br><br>
        <table style="margin: auto; text-align: center; font-size: 0.9em; border-collapse: collapse;" border="1">
          <tr><th>&nbsp; Hypothesis &nbsp;</th><th>&nbsp; Prior &nbsp;</th><th>&nbsp; Likelihood &nbsp;</th><th>&nbsp; Unnorm. post. &nbsp;</th><th>&nbsp; Posterior &nbsp;</th></tr>
          <tr><td>type A</td><td><br><br></td><td></td><td></td><td></td></tr>
          <tr><td>type B</td><td><br><br></td><td></td><td></td><td></td></tr>
          <tr><td>type C</td><td><br><br></td><td></td><td></td><td></td></tr>
        </table>
        <br>
        Normalizer: ____________
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```

:::

:::{.notes}
**Solution (a)**

| Hypothesis | Prior | Likelihood | Unnorm. post. | Posterior |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| type A | 10/30 = 1/3 | 3/5 | 1/5 = 12/60 | 12/28 = 3/7 |
| type B | 5/30 = 1/6 | 1/10 | 1/60 | 1/28 |
| type C | 15/30 = 1/2 | 1/2 | 1/4 = 15/60 | 15/28 |

Normalizer: 12/60 + 1/60 + 15/60 = 28/60 = 7/15 ≈ 0.4667
:::

## Group Question 2 {.scrollable}
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}

```{python}
def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="blue-box">
        <p>
        b. Find the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate for the type of the coin. Explain your reasoning.
        <br>
        <br>
        <br>
        <br>
        <br>
        c. Is the prior in this problem informative? Explain your reasoning.
        <br>
        <br>
        <br>
        <br>
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```

:::

:::{.notes}
**Solution (b)**: The MAP is coin type C, because it has the highest posterior probability (15/28 ≈ 0.536).

**Solution (c)**: Yes. The prior (1/3, 1/6, 1/2) is not uniform. It uses what we know about how many coins of each type are in the bag, so it is informative.

:::
